title: Compassion, Part 3: To Hell and Back Again
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating compassion by acknowledging and embracing our own suffering as well as that of others. This involves being willing to feel and understand the pain and imperfections of ourselves and others, rather than trying to limit or compartmentalize them. By doing so, we can find a happiness that includes the full human experience of suffering, which requires patience, practice, and a willingness to connect with others' struggles.

First, of course, we have to actually notice that someone is suffering, or that we are suffering, and if we pay attention we might realize that we don't notice a lot of the time.

Bummer."

And yet how do we understand this wanting happiness and wanting freedom from suffering?
Practicing compassion, does that mean we need to defer our happiness for a time and turn towards suffering?

Because it's a practice.
To open and fully feel the suffering in us and around us takes practice.

There's an opening and a turning.
The light gets in through the cracks.
It sure does take a lot of patience.
Here's an example, a pretty benign example really, of a limited compassion.
When I noticed that I'd done this I was so disappointed in myself and then I had to practice compassion for me.
It's okay to be disappointed.
Somebody I'm studying with had sudden and terrible news: her mother, who had been going along fine as far as she knew, has stage four cancer pretty much all over.
In her lymph, in her stomach, in her lungs, everywhere.
The doctors aren't even sure where it started.
I saw this in a message and I actually noticed that this was suffering.
So that's good.
And I realized I should call her.

In this case I did.

That's good.

It didn't feel very connected.
It was clear that she was glad that I had reached out, that I had called.

"Hi, I know I'm supposed to call you now.
How are you?
Is it okay?
How can I help?"
But I didn't really contemplate or feel into what that might be like.
I didn't take a few moments or a few breaths to be curious about what would it be like if my mother, who is also alive and doing well as far as I know, suddenly was on the edge of death.
How would this feel?
How would it really feel?
And after I hung up I realized I hadn't even really asked how she was feeling or given her space to express that, or asked how it was to receive this terrible news.
I just focused the conversation on the tangible details.
Where does your family live?
What support do you have?
Are you going to go to Ohio next week?
These kinds of questions.
And it was not bad.
It was okay.
She was glad for the call, I'm sure.
And she'll probably thank me for it later.
But I didn't really feel like compassion.
And I felt pretty sad afterwards, which maybe meant I was beginning or taking another small step in the journey of compassion.
But I could notice that I'd had a superficial conversation with someone that I really care about, about something like the worst possible thing.
Just yakking away about logistics.
Well, the Tibetan Buddhist tradition, and I'm sure it's in other parts of Buddhism as well, but this is where I learned about it, has an interesting practice to help us with this.
My goodness.
More compassion required.
I forgot the book.
Well, I'll just tell you about it.
It's the practice of contemplating the Buddhist hell realms.

And on the bottom of this stack, and I'm pretty sure it is there, stacked that way, just like in Judeo-Christian thought, where the hells are below and the heavens are above.
But it's a little different from Christianity, in that the hells are realms of great suffering, but nobody is in any of these realms permanently.
Everything is always changing in Buddhist thought.
But depending on causes and conditions, you may be reborn in any one of these six realms.
And who knows how the early Buddhists saw this, the sort of pre-modern people studying Buddhism who worked all this out?
Did they see these mythological realms as real, in the way we were always wondering, "Well, that's not really real, so it's not important"?
Or do they have not the same idea that we have of real and unreal?
Probably the latter.
So maybe we don't have a way of understanding the mindset they brought to this.
But the contemplation is to practice really imagining what it would be like to be in these hell realms.
And there are, I think, like 13 principal ones and lots of minor ones, and they have very graphic descriptions.
I was going to read you one of the descriptions, but I'll just try my best to remember.
One of them is that you're lying on a table, and you can't move, but you're conscious, and you can feel everything perfectly.
And a sort of devil-type figure shows up and draws lines across your body, very carefully draws all these lines, and then gets out a big saw.
No kidding, this is traditional Buddhist stuff.
And he cuts you apart on all these lines, and it feels the way it would feel to us.
And then you heal, and they start over again, so they're all fairly cyclical like that.
There's another one which I wanted to focus on and have us practice with a little bit.
They're strange and gross on purpose.
The other one is you feel very lonely and disconnected, and you're at the bottom of a hill.
At the top of the hill is a wonderful person, someone you wish you were with and wish you knew.
And you're naked.
I think you're naked in most of these.
I don't know if they have clothes in hell.
And so you're drawn to climb up this hill to find this person.
Unfortunately, the surface of the hill is exactly like a really sharp cheese grater.
It's the grater hell, I don't know what they call it.

And so as you climb up, you're being hurt, but you're so drawn, you want this love and connection or whatever it is with this person, that you keep going, and keep going, and keep going, and you make it to the top of the hill.
Know what happens when you get to the top of the hill?
Of course, the person is not there.
And then you fall and slide back down, and then they appear again, stuff like that.

So I don't know if we can relate to these images, but it's an interesting encouragement to really contemplate, and really breathe with, and really wonder what it is like for beings, myself and other beings, to be really stuck in painful situations, and stuck there for a long time.
Eventually, you work through your karmic whatever, and you get out, and you get reborn into another realm.
So just for the sake of completeness, here are the other realms.

Second is the realm of hunger, the hungry realm, which is mostly inhabited by the hungry ghosts, who are creatures that have these huge distended bellies, because they're starving. [unclear: "And next, as thick as pencils"], and they're surrounded by really tasty looking food, but they can't eat it.
They both try to eat it, but they can't swallow, so they're always hungry.
And if we're thinking about this in a little more symbolic way, this is us when we just can't seem to be satisfied.
We just can't seem to get what we want, even though it's right in front of us somehow.
It's never enough, right?
So the realm of the hungry ghosts is an engine of capitalism, though.
We need that.
So there's the hell realms, the hungry realm, the hungry ghosts realm, and there's the animal realm.
And I get the impression the early Buddhists didn't see nature as an ecological and beautiful thing, because the way they represented this idea is with animals.
But the animals in the brutality and nature red in tooth and claw mode, animals competing and fighting.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** And in the animal realm, there's a lack of judgment and restraint and a lot of aggression.
So we have this, right?
We have aggression.
We lose our restraint.
The fourth realm is the realm of arrogance and anger, which is inhabited by these god-ish creatures called the [unclear: "shuras"].
They're more or less like the Titans in Greek mythology.
Not quite gods, but not quite people.
Again, nothing here is immortal, but these guys live a very long time.
They're like, I don't know, type A business executives or something like that.
They're really effective.
They're really fast moving.
They're very selfish, very competitive.
They know how to get stuff done, but they're stuck.
They're stuck on the treadmill of never finishing their lists.
They can potentially be virtuous, though.
They can do good works, but they're enslaved to their delusions and ego.
The fifth realm is us.
We made it.
The human realm.

This is seen as the perfect realm for practice because while we are subject to all of these echoes and issues from the four realms below us, we're not that stuck in all that suffering, because we possess the possibility to understand and transcend and transform suffering.
But the human realm, unlike most of the other realms, is characterized by a very brief period of time.
In most of the other realms you're there for a very, very long time.
I don't know how many years, but a long time.
But human life is short.
Life is brief.
But because it's brief, we wake up to it and we recognize that it's precious.
It's a precious opportunity.
The basic idea is that in the human realm we have just enough suffering to motivate ourselves for practice and to use as energy and information for practice.
So part of the turning in the human realm is to learn to appreciate our suffering.
Be glad for it, actually.
This is our material.
This is how we wake up.
So the human realm is the perfect place for the practice of compassion.
Perfect.
We can feel suffering, but hopefully, at least some of the time, not be so caught by it that we can't hold it in a wise way, in a compassionate way, and wake up.
So it seems like these are getting progressively better, but interestingly the next realm is the realm of the heavens.
And this is seen as an undesirable realm for us.

It's seen as undesirable because in the heavenly realms, and there are many different manifestations just like in the hell realms, the problem for those beings who are semi-gods called devas is that they're so blissed out and happy that they're in a daze.
They can't practice.
And the happiness they feel is so flimsy.
They're caught in it, but it's not quite satisfying.
So they're always seeking new ways to bliss out and hang out in what I learned recently psychologists call the hedonic treadmill.
We can unpack that later.
They're stuck in the hedonic treadmill.
But they're loving it.
They're having a good time.
And of course we have some of this too, right?
We have this desire to be in the heavenly realms.
We have the desire to check out, to indulge in something.

But we don't want to be stuck in the heavenly realms because we can't really practice there.

So it's interesting that sometimes we are in a balanced human perspective, appreciating the preciousness of human life, the opportunity to feel the human emotions from love to sadness, the opportunity to be fully ourselves, the opportunity to help others and to grow and to wake up.
But we're always touched by these other five realms.
The hell realms of feeling stuck, so trapped in our suffering, burning up in pain.
The hungry realms where we can't seem to quite get enough.
The animal realms where we're aggressive.
And the arrogant realms where we are sure we're right.
So our task is to feel all of this and bring some wisdom to it so that we can practice compassion.
Practice compassion.
And practice wisdom.
And learn directly through our own experience how much better that is.
How much better that deeply is than just getting what we want.
Than just being right or just being wrong.
So I don't know if the saws and the iron grater hell help us, but I think it actually is part of our work to contemplate the difficult things in life.
Not just as an idea, or just something we might have to deal with later, but as a felt experience.
This sounds grim, but it's our mindfulness bell.

And then we can have a little bit of conversation.
So: remembering the preciousness and the rarity of human life.
Remembering the inevitability of death.
Death is certain.
Only the time of death is uncertain.
Remembering the absolute inevitability of suffering.
This is a part of life.
Even though we may hope for less suffering, and I hope we all have less suffering, we can't avoid suffering.
And fourthly, recognizing the indelible power of our actions.
Our actions of thought and body and mind.
Everything we do or think has an effect.
And helps beings as they try to move through these realms.
Or maybe hurts beings as they try to move through these realms.
So that's the next installment of compassion.
What do you think?
What's on your mind?
How is it for you when you're faced with somebody suffering?
Do you find it easy to really feel that?
Or do you find there are ways that the mind disengages or limits it a little bit?
Or how does it work?
**Participant:** Curiously, I was identifying with the [unclear: "chiefs greater realm"].
It seems like one of the least pleasant ones to be described.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** That's just illuminating right there in itself.
Yeah, we want that.
We want whatever that is up there.

That's great, but how many times have I really hurt someone?

**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, the power of our actions, right, that fourth one.
And that doesn't mean we can't celebrate when we've helped somebody.
It's a beautiful world.
But then maybe one of the ways that we avoid full engagement is that we get into this dualistic idea of, "Oh, I must be a good person."

We're just a person in this vast dance.
Yeah, yeah, I remember that.
Any other thoughts?

**Participant:** Well, I think that one way you can disengage is deciding to fix it.

**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Right.
Yeah.

Yeah.
Anyone else relate to that, not just trying to fix people and fix yourself?
Oh, yeah.
**Participant:** Yeah?
I find it pretty easy to come to that place of compassion.

That sounds like I'm over the top.
I'm not.
But I easily can feel and pull and want to.
And I've been reading a lot of Zen stuff about this tradition.
And I really like Norman Fischer's talk on being a priest that's online on our website.
He uses the word obligation, of being obligated to be there for others, to walk in their shoes.
When I first heard that word obligation, I thought, wow, isn't that more of an aspiration than an obligation?
And I've just been sitting with that word for the last two or three weeks and thinking, yeah, that's what we're here for.
That's what I'm here for.
That's what I want.
But it's still a balance.
So is there an obligation to take care of yourself?
Yeah, but that's a little more difficult to pay attention to.
But that's a good practice for me right now.
Thank you.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Okay.
Thank you for your comments and your listening.

And of course these are all conversations I hope will continue in the lobby and in the garden and when we run into each other in other places, just to support each other in studying these things and practicing these things.
It's so easy for other kinds of conversations to dominate.
That's okay.
But please let's continue studying compassion and wisdom.
Somehow, the result of our choices and many other people's choices have supported us all those years.
Somehow the result of that is we ended up here.
So here's the obligation piece.
There's some obligation there, I think.
Some responsibility to take care of the world.
And with this kind of wisdom.
Okay, thanks.
